title: The purple thread
hookLine: Epictetus wants to be the purple stripe in the robe, the small part that makes the rest beautiful (Discourses 1.2)

lines: I WANT TO BE THAT STRIPE.
cards: A Roman senator's tunic was mostly plain wool, with broad bands of purple running down it. That purple came from sea snails, crushed by the thousands, and it cost a fortune.
A narrow strip of color on a big garment, and the part everyone saw. Epictetus told his students he wanted to be the purple in the garment. Not the whole cloak.
Not even most of it. Just the thin bright strip that makes the rest look good.

teach.b: It comes in the same chapter as yesterday, Discourses book one, chapter two, wrapped around a story about a senator named Helvidius Priscus. The emperor Vespasian sent word: don't come to the senate.
Helvidius answered, more or less: you can remove me, but while I'm a senator, I go. Then go, and keep quiet. Don't ask my opinion, and I'll keep quiet.
But I have to ask it. Then I have to say what seems right. Then I'll have you killed.
And Helvidius said: did I ever tell you I couldn't die? You do your part, and I'll do mine.

teach.h: WHAT GOOD DID ONE MAN DO?
teach.b: Then the practical question: what good did one man do?

teach.h: THE STRIPE SHOWS WHAT A CLOAK CAN BE.
teach.b: What good does the purple do the cloak? It doesn't keep anyone warmer. It stands out, and it sets an example for the rest.
He'd used the image a few lines earlier.

teach.h: YOU CHOOSE WHICH THREAD TO BE.
teach.b: Someone tells him: be like everyone else, just one thread among the many. Fine, Epictetus says, for someone who sees himself that way. But I want to be the purple.
He isn't saying everyone has to be heroic, or that the plain wool is worthless. A cloak is mostly wool.
He's saying each person decides what kind of thread to be, and that one bright strand changes how the whole garment looks.
The week in one breath: willingly, carry three, a real classroom, the gift of use, not even Zeus, I know my price, and now the purple thread.

how: Readers of the Stoics often keep the image of the purple stripe as a reminder that one person's conduct can set the tone for a room, a family or a workplace.

games.q: you're Helvidius Priscus. the emperor says: come to the senate, but keep quiet. what do you answer?
o: then don't ask my opinion; if you ask, I'll say what seems right.
games.why: Helvidius said he'd speak if asked, and when threatened with death, said: you do your part, I'll do mine.

practice: Picture one ordinary moment coming up, a meeting, a family dinner, a line at the store, as a plain cloak with everyone going along.

Then look for where a thin bright thread could run through it: the honest answer, the kind word, the person who stays calm. You don't have to change the whole room, only see the one strand you could be.

wordCard.voice: Helvidius Priscus. The senator who defied an emperor and kept his own character; the small part that shows the rest what it could be.

orig.note: Greek porphyra: purple, the costly dye; Epictetus wrote nothing himself, and Arrian's notes of his teaching are in Greek.

carryVoice: Your line: the bright strand. A cloak is mostly wool, and that's all right. Day three hundred ninety-two, and a week done.
